title: KV cache eviction, paging, and prefix reuse deep dive - Lynx Solutions
summary: Redwood SE walked Lynx through KV cache architecture, eviction heuristics, paging strategies to CPU/NVMe, and prefix reuse best practices. Key outcomes: identify likely LRU thrashing due to variable session lengths and long-context churn; recommended experiments for cache sizing, pinning hot prefixes, and controlled paging tests; agreed to run a 24h benchmark with trace-level KV metrics and to share diagnostic logs.
action_items: Jordan Li - provide KV cache diag script and metrics dashboard link (due: 2026-12-24)
Elena Cruz - share representative session traces and 24h traffic sample (due: 2026-12-23)
Samir Patel - enable redwood debug logging for node-3 and attach nvme/pmem stats (due: 2026-12-22)
next_steps: Redwood to run a 24h bench with Lynx traffic sample and report eviction rates and paging counts
Customer to confirm target SLOs for 95th/99th latencies and retention policy for KV cache entries
Schedule follow-up to review bench results w/ live logs (proposed 2026-12-28)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel, Jordan Li (Redwood); Rajiv Menon, Elena Cruz, Samir Patel (Lynx)

00:00 - Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick agenda — deep dive into KV cache eviction/paging and prefix reuse, we want to get to root cause of your eviction spikes.
00:18 - Rajiv Menon: Yep, thanks Maya. We've been see-ing spikes in tail latency when sessions go long, and eviction counts blow up, which then causes regen penalties.
00:30 - Jordan Li: Right, and from the logs you sent we can see a lot of small sessions interleaving with a handful of very long contexts, so we suspect working set thrash.
01:05 - Elena Cruz: Just to clarify, our typical session distribution is: 60% short 50-200 tokens, 30% medium 200-1k, and 10% long 1k-6k. The long ones are driving up kv usage.
01:22 - Jordan Li: That matches; our runtime maintains a per-model KV cache sharded by GPU. Eviction policy defaults to LRU with fixed per-shard capacity, and when a long-context stream hits it, the prefix tokens occupy a lot of entries and push out hot short-session prefixes — classic LRU thrash.
01:40 - Samir Patel: Can you explain why prefix reuse doesn't save us here? We thought reuse of earlier tokens would prevent regen.
01:50 - Jordan Li: Prefix reuse helps when the same prefix reappears often. But two things: one, our cache key includes session id + token offset by default, so identical text across sessions doesn't hit unless you normalize keying to text-based prefix IDs; two, long contexts append many unique offsets so they monopolize slots.
02:20 - Rajiv Menon: So is the fix just increase cache size?
02:26 - Jordan Li: That's one lever. Increasing per-shard capacity reduces eviction pressure, but it's not linear — memory is finite on GPU. We recommend a combined approach: pinning hot prefixes, normalized keying for cross-session reuse, and smarter eviction like segmented LRU or frequency-aware (e.g., LIRS) to keep frequently re-used prefixes.
03:05 - Maya Patel: Also consider TTL for long prefixes; if a prefix hasn't been accessed in X minutes, evict earlier. But be careful with long-lived sessions where TTL could evict mid-session if not accessed recently.
03:22 - Elena Cruz: You mentioned paging — what's the cost of paging KV entries to CPU or NVMe?
03:30 - Jordan Li: Paging is viable as a tiered cache: hot entries on GPU, warm on host RAM, cold on NVMe. Paging to host RAM has modest latency penalty (tens of microseconds to low single-digit ms) but to NVMe can be tens to hundreds of ms depending on access pattern and device. The runtime supports async prefetching for predicted next tokens which helps hide NVMe latency for sequential reads but random accesses can be bad.
04:05 - Samir Patel: Our infra is air-gapped in VPC with limited NVMe capacity on nodes — any special config?
04:12 - Jordan Li: That's fine; you can enable host paging only and tune page size and eviction thresholds. For air-gapped, ensure permissions for debug and low-level tracing are set so we can collect page fault rates.
04:38 - Rajiv Menon: Is quantization affecting cache size or eviction?
04:43 - Jordan Li: Yes — aggressive quantization reduces per-key size so you can store more entries for same memory footprint, but there are tradeoffs: some quant formats increase CPU decode time on page faults, and certain quantization can change attention kernel behaviors causing slightly different KV key encoding or lengths. We typically recommend 4-bit quant for large models for a good balance.
05:10 - Elena Cruz: What about prefix reuse strategies? We have ~200 customers and some share similar prompts; can we dedupe across sessions?
05:20 - Jordan Li: You can normalize keys by hashing canonicalized text rather than session offset; that allows cross-session reuse. Caveat: you must ensure privacy boundaries — don't mix per-tenant prefixes unless you design tenant-aware key namespaces. Also, canonicalization must be deterministic and cheap; you might limit canonicalization to the first N tokens of a prefix.
06:00 - Maya Patel: Another trick is prefix pinning: identify a small set of highly reused prefixes and pin them in GPU memory to prevent eviction. Pinning reduces effective capacity for others, so pick top 1-3% by hit-rate.
06:28 - Rajiv Menon: How do we measure hit rate vs regen cost?
06:34 - Jordan Li: We surface per-prefix hit/miss counters and regeneration latency; multiply miss rate by avg regen token cost to estimate tail cost. Jordan: I'll provide a diagnostic script that computes working set heatmap.
07:05 - Elena Cruz: We also saw a pattern where after rolling deploys eviction spikes. Any suggestions there?
07:12 - Jordan Li: Rolling deploys change model shard mapping and invalidate some pinned sets; we'd recommend a warmup step — replay a small traffic sample to warm KV before cutover or use gradual traffic shifting.
07:36 - Samir Patel: Paging thresholds — are they static? We saw paging spikes at 200k entries.
07:43 - Jordan Li: Defaults are conservative. Tune thresholds based on observed working set. Also consider adaptive thresholds: if miss latency rises, proactively shrink shard caps and offload cold entries.
08:10 - Rajiv Menon: Is there support for time-based windowed caches for long context sessions?
08:16 - Jordan Li: Yes, session-affine caches can hold recent N tokens per session in a ring buffer (fast path) while longer history lives in a separate warm store; this prevents huge unique offsets from thrashing global cache.
08:40 - Elena Cruz: Any gotchas with batching? We batch at 64 which gives good throughput, but latency spikes interact with cache misses.
08:48 - Jordan Li: Batching increases throughput but hides per-request variability — a cache miss inside a batch can stall many queries. Consider dynamic batch breakouts when predicted miss is high, or prioritize low-latency requests in separate lanes.
09:15 - Maya Patel: Let's go through recommended experiments we discussed: 1) run bench with 24h sample and current config, 2) enable key-normalization for a subset of prefixes, 3) try pinning top N prefixes, 4) run paging-only to host RAM to measure penalty.
09:35 - Rajiv Menon: Sounds good. For the bench we'll need the diag script and exact metrics to collect.
09:42 - Jordan Li: I'll share the script — it'll emit eviction counts per-shard, page fault counts, per-prefix hit/miss, regen latency histograms, and mem usage.
10:05 - Elena Cruz: On security: we need to confirm that cross-session prefix hash doesn't leak tenant data and meets our SSO/PEP policies.
10:12 - Maya Patel: Yes, do not enable cross-tenant reuse without tenant namespacing. Also Redwood can provide docs on how keys are computed and how to opt into canonicalization in a tenant-aware way.
10:34 - Samir Patel: Any immediate config tweaks we can try?
10:38 - Jordan Li: Short-term: increase per-shard cap by 10-20% if GPU headroom exists; enable host RAM paging (not NVMe) for a week of monitoring; enable per-prefix hit logging; and pin top 1% prefixes.
11:05 - Rajiv Menon: Ok that seems actionable.
11:12 - Maya Patel: Recap and next steps: Jordan will drop the diag scripts and dashboard; Lynx will send sample traces and enable debug logging; Redwood will run the bench and come back with a report and recommendations.
11:30 - Elena Cruz: Thanks all, looking forward to the bench results.
11:40 - Meeting end.
